                                INITIAL BRIEF OF INTERVENORS
          BOHKERS, LLC – SERIES 119 AND KIELLA LAND INVESTMENTS LTD.

           Intervenors BOHKERS, LLC – Series 119 and Kiella Land Investments Ltd. (collectively,

“Intervenors”) respectfully submit this Initial Brief and request that the Public Utility Commission

of Texas (“Commission”) deny approval of any route containing Link A-42 (formerly Link A-4)

and instead approve a route that avoids Link A-42, including Applicants’ preferred Route 894 or

another non-A-42 route supported by the evidentiary record.

           Intervenors do not oppose the need for the Bell County East to Big Hill 765-kV

transmission line project generally.1 They do, however, oppose all routes containing Link A-42—

including Routes 767, 771, 910, 911, 913, 914, 915, 916, and 1031—and any other route or link

that crosses or adversely impacts Intervenors’ property.2 However, the record in this proceeding

compels rejection of any route containing Link A-42.

           1. Ongoing and planned developments along A-42, including MeadowLake, strongly
              weigh against the approval of any route containing the A-42 Link.

           Ongoing and planned developments must be considered in selecting a transmission line

route. The Commission considers impacts to both existing and planned uses. 3 Where feasible,

routes are to be adjusted to reduce impacts to land uses. 4 However, Applicants did not look into

preliminary plats, construction plans, permits, municipal utility districts (or “MUDs”) which are

used to facilitate development, to determine if there were any developments within the study area

of the Project.5

           Various parcels that A-42 bisects and/or adjoins, are currently the sites of ongoing

redevelopment, which is in various states of completion. For example, Applicants stipulated that

they were unaware that another intervenor, BKV Land Holdings I, LLC, (“BKV”) planned to

develop its property along A42, and, as such did not consider the development in the routing

process.6 BKV’s planned development is a future development.7

           Separately, Intervenors established through Scott Kiella’s direct testimony and exhibits

that MeadowLake is a concrete, advanced master-planned community that Link A-42 would bisect

and impair. 8 MeadowLake is planned to include residences, multiple amenity centers, open

parkland, an extensive trail system, naturally rolling hills, grassland, an expansive lake system,

and multiple road frontage and access points. Kiella Direct at 8:129–136. The development is

designed around a future Temple ISD elementary school and is anticipated to include two lakes,

trails, swimming pools, tennis courts, park areas, community amenities, and green space. 9 The

MeadowLake Master-Planned Community, located south of FM 93 and west of Old State Highway

95 / Little River Road.11

        Intervenors have been actively pursuing this development with the City of Temple, and the

City has already approved sewer lift stations that would service parcels that A-42 would bisect,

annexed parts of the development into the city, and will annex the remainder of the development

this calendar year.12 At the time of his direct, Mr. Kiella testified Phase III of MeadowLake was

already approved by the City of Temple’s City Council, that the planned development’s zoning

was approved, and the plat was approved in May of 2026.13

        MeadowLake is not speculative future development entitled to little weight. It is a concrete,

advanced development with approved zoning, approved plats, approved infrastructure, millions of

dollars in investment, and active municipal coordination spanning multiple phases. The evidence

of its advancement far exceeds mere intention—it reflects binding governmental approvals and

substantial capital commitment.

        Certainly BKV and MeadowLake are not the only impacted developments in the works

along the A-42 link. The City of Temple, Temple Independent School District, and Academy

Independent School District have passed a resolution “expressing strong opposition to” what is

now known as Link A-42, previously Link A-4, because it would negatively impact existing and

planned developments for single-family dwellings, schools, parks, and recreation areas after they

purchases, and the development of schools and neighborhoods to support the continued residential

growth of the community.”14 For this reason, they described proposed routes containing the A-42

link as “incompatible with the long-term community development” and “undermining the strategic

and financial investments made by the City and the districts.15

        As a result, the Commission should weigh these ongoing and planned future developments

strongly against any route which would include the A-42 link.

        2. No expert witness in this proceeding—whether retained by Applicants, Staff, or
           any intervenor—has identified any route containing Link A-42 as a preferred or
           best-meets route.

        Two groups of experts not paid by intervenors—Applicants and Staff—arrived at Routes

894 and 487, respectively, as their best-meets routes.16 Neither route contains Link A-42.

        Applicants have consistently recommended Route 894 as their preferred, best-meets

route.17 Even after the numerous filings, exhibits, and direct testimonies filed in this case, Ms.

Cooley confirmed Route 894 remains viable and constructible, and Ms. Perkins confirmed Route

894 remains Applicants' best-meets recommendation.18 Route 894 does not contain Link A-42.

        PUC Staff recommends Route 487. 19 PUC Staff witness John Poole testified he

recommends Route 487 as the best-meets route. 20 Mr. Poole considered Route 296 as another

favorable non-A-42 route—his second-place route, very close behind 487 and above Route 894—

487 is the best route after continuing review.22 Mr. Poole clarified he is not advocating selection

of Route 296 or other routes besides Route 487.23

           Moreover, expert witnesses hired by other intervenors recommend Routes 894, 487, 392,

or 296—all non-A-42 routes.24 Hopkins confirmed that Route 894 remains his best-meets route

after corrections. 25 Andrews filed testimony continuing to support Route 894. 26 Jason Buntz

confirmed his route recommendation is Route 894.27 No expert testimony or expert report in the

record identifies any A-42 route as preferred.

           3. Routing Criteria dictates the Route should not pass through Link A-42 when other
              routes are available which better satisfy all applicable routing criteria.

           Link A-42 would bisect and fragment Intervenors’ property, destroying the cohesive

MeadowLake Master-Planned Community—a development with municipal zoning approvals,

approved plats, and millions of dollars of invested capital—while non-A-42 routes are available

that do not cross Intervenors’ property and satisfy all applicable routing criteria.28

                    A. Link A-42 fails to parallel existing compatible rights-of-way and property
                       lines.

           Commission Rule 25.101(b)(3)(B) directs that transmission line routes shall, to the extent

reasonable, parallel existing compatible rights-of-way, other compatible rights-of-way such as

roads, and property lines. Applicants' own witnesses acknowledged that Applicants attempt to

only a small fraction of its length—the remainder cuts across property without regard to

boundaries, fragmenting ownership and development potential.

           Link A-42 does precisely what Applicants themselves seek to avoid—it bisects multiple

parcels and fragments a cohesive master-planned community. Link A-42 would devastate the

MeadowLake development by running directly through Intervenors' parcels:

               •    Parcel 3347: Currently agricultural but part of the master-planned community. A-
                    42 would run straight through the middle and divide it in near-equal halves.31 Parcel
                    3347 is within Phase III of MeadowLake, for which City Council approved Planned
                    Development zoning approximately November 2025 and the plat was approved
                    May 2026.32

               •    Parcel 3348: Currently agricultural but part of the master-planned community. A-
                    42 would bisect it, leaving approximately two-thirds on one side and one-third on
                    the other.33 Parcel 3348 is also within Phase III.34

               •    Parcels 3351 and 3352: Currently agricultural but part of the master-planned
                    community. A-42 would run immediately north and separate them from contiguous
                    Parcel 3353. 35 These parcels are in Phase II, for which the City of Temple has
                    approved the sewer lift station.36

               •    Parcel 3353: Currently agricultural but part of the master-planned community. A-
                    42 would bisect it and cut off the southern portion of Parcel 3353, along with
                    contiguous Parcels 3351 and 3352, from the rest of Parcel 3353.37

        A high-voltage 765-kV transmission line along A-42 and through MeadowLake would take

up property intended for housing and amenities, jeopardize financial feasibility, and leave the

community with a high-voltage power line instead of planned lakes, parks, and amenities.38

        Moreover, MeadowLake is not the only property or development that Link A-42 would

bisect. Of A-42’s 52,715-foot total length, none parallels existing electric transmission lines,

railroads, public roads or highways, or pipelines, and only 8,525 feet parallels apparent property

boundaries. Instead, A-42 meanders through parcels.

                    B. Routes containing Link A-42 go against stated community values and
                       impede recreational and park areas.

        The City of Temple, Temple ISD, and Academy ISD have further expressed their strong

opposition to A-42/A-4 through Resolution No. 2025-0236-R because of its significant negative

impacts on existing and planned residential neighborhoods, schools, and parks. 39 The City of

Temple, Temple Independent School District, and Academy Independent School District jointly

adopted Resolution No. 2025-0236-R, which supports the Bell County East to Big Hill 765-kV

Project generally but strongly opposes A-42 "due to significant negative impacts on existing and

planned residential neighborhoods, schools, and parks/recreation areas."40 The Resolution states

the City and school districts have "invested significant public resources in planning, infrastructure

installation, land purchases, and the development of schools and neighborhoods to support

continued residential growth," and that A-42 (formerly known as A-4) is "incompatible with long-

term community development vision and would reduce quality of life for residents and students

while undermining those strategic and financial investments."41

        The statutory routing criteria specifically require consideration of "community values" and

"recreational and park areas." TEX. UTIL. CODE § 37.056(c)(4)(A)–(B). The opposition of the

municipality in which Link A-42 would be located, together with the school districts serving that

area, reflects the community's judgment that A-42 is incompatible with community values, planned

neighborhoods, schools, and recreational areas. This official governmental opposition is entitled

to substantial weight. Mr. Poole himself acknowledged that the community feedback in this case

included both concern about existing land use and future land use.42

        MeadowLake is designed around a future Temple ISD elementary school and anticipates

lakes, trails, swimming pools, tennis courts, park areas, and green space.43 A high-voltage 765-kV

line through A-42 would directly conflict with these recreational and park-related uses that PURA

directs the Commission to protect.

                    C. Prudent Avoidance weighs against routes containing A-42.

        As Mr. Poole discussed in his testimony, the way to prudently avoid or limit exposure to

EMFs is to propose routes that minimize the number of habitable structures in close proximity

with fewer habitable structures within 500 feet being a better outcome.44 The prudent avoidance

comparison should give some weight to large scale subdivision developments, regardless of the

progress of construction at the time, with more weight being given to developments that are further

along.45

        A-42 has more habitable structures and greater potential exposure. Link A-42 itself has 11

existing habitable structures.46 When the MeadowLake development is considered—197 dwelling

units in Phase I alone, plus hundreds more in subsequent phases—the number of habitable

structures affected by A-42 will increase dramatically.

        Additionally, in the middle of the MeadowLake development there is a planned Temple

ISD elementary school.47 Schools are considered habitable structures in a routing analysis.48 If

possible, Applicants avoid schools.49 This is because of a concern for the health and safety of

students who might be at a school. 50 Under the doctrine of prudent avoidance, schools are

important to avoid because, unlike a smaller structure that may have 10 or less persons, schools

will likely have large numbers of persons, namely children, inside.51

        Given these habitable structures, the doctrine of prudent avoidance weighs against any

route containing Link A-42 being approved.

                             VIII. CONCLUSION AND PRAYER

        Ms. Perkins testified that Oncor is "fine with any route using application route links in a

forward-progressing manner from endpoint to endpoint" if it is constructible.52 Multiple non-A-42

routes are available in the record. The Commission need not select a route that disrupts the entire

City of Temple’s development plans, including by fragmenting a 229-acre master-planned

community, when alternatives exist that avoid this harm entirely.

        Thus, when the Commission considers which route, if any, to approve, the Commission

should weigh the various factors it is to consider against any route which includes the A-42 link.

        WHEREFORE, PREMISES CONSIDERED, Intervenors BOHKERS, LLC – Series

119 and Kiella Land Investments Ltd. respectfully request that the Administrative Law Judge

recommend, and the Public Utility Commission of Texas order, as follows:

        1. That the Commission deny approval of any route containing Link A-42, including
           Routes 767, 771, 910, 911, 913, 914, 915, 916, 1031, and any other route utilizing Link
           A-42;

        2. That the Commission approve a route that does not include Link A-42, supported by
           the evidentiary record;

        3. That the Commission issue such other and further relief as is just and proper.
